metadata.title: US appeals court weighs block on Kennedy's vaccine panel appointments

sources.news_title: Appeals Court Questions Scope of Judge’s Order Blocking RFK Jr.’s Vaccine Panel Appointments
sources.text:
A federal appeals court pressed attorneys Tuesday over whether a lower-court order blocking 13 members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel went too far, with one judge questioning what injury justified such “intrusive relief.”
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
A federal appeals court on Tuesday questioned whether a Massachusetts judge exceeded the appropriate scope of judicial relief when he blocked most of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s appointments to the federal panel that advises the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on vaccines.
During oral arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, one judge repeatedly pressed lawyers representing medical organizations challenging Kennedy’s appointments to identify the specific harm that justified preventing the advisers from serving.
“What is the harm that needs to be redressed, or that would justify this kind of intrusive relief?” the judge asked during the Oct. 6 hearing, according to Reuters.
The Trump administration is asking the appeals court to stay the portion of U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy’s March 16 order that suspended the appointments of 13 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, or ACIP.
The committee has not met since Murphy’s ruling, and scheduled meetings have been canceled while the litigation continues.
“We’re asking the court to vacate the order on the appointments so that the secretary can reconstitute the committee and get it back to work,” Justice Department attorney Matthew Zorn told the First Circuit panel Tuesday.
Zorn argued that the plaintiffs — including the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical and public-health organizations — would not suffer a legally cognizable injury simply because Kennedy’s appointees were permitted to serve.
He also argued that appointments to an advisory committee are not themselves final agency actions subject to review under the Administrative Procedure Act.
Murphy’s March order went considerably beyond the appointments issue.
The judge stayed a January 2026 memorandum that revised the federal childhood immunization schedule, suspended the appointments of 13 ACIP members selected in June 2025, September 2025 and January 2026, and stayed all votes taken by the reconstituted committee.
Murphy concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their argument that the committee violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act, or FACA, which requires federal advisory panels to be fairly balanced and their members to be appropriately qualified.
Kennedy had removed all 17 previous ACIP members in June 2025, saying the panel suffered from conflicts of interest and that a complete overhaul was necessary to restore public confidence.
He subsequently appointed new members, including physician and mRNA vaccine technology pioneer Dr. Robert Malone and Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor Retsef Levi.
Murphy determined that 13 of Kennedy’s selections were likely appointed through a process that failed to satisfy federal requirements governing advisory committees.
The American Public Health Association said the ruling also blocked the administration’s January overhaul of the childhood vaccination schedule, reversed changes affecting COVID-19 vaccine recommendations and stayed changes involving the hepatitis B vaccine.
The administration is currently appealing the portion of the ruling dealing with ACIP appointments rather than every component of Murphy’s order.
Zorn told the First Circuit that the practical effect of the ruling has been to disable the committee.
“The practical matter of this case is, the secretary wants to get the ACIP back to work, and we’re being told that if he reconstitutes any committee, it’s going to be right back in court,” Zorn said.
Attorney Andrew Pincus, representing the medical organizations, defended Murphy’s ruling as the “least intrusive relief possible.”
Pincus argued that Kennedy remained free under the order to appoint a lawfully constituted committee, including potentially reappointing some of the same individuals along with new members.
“If that constellation of people was lawful, his order would not prohibit that ACIP from going forward,” Pincus said.
The appeals judges appeared particularly interested in whether the plaintiffs could establish a concrete injury stemming merely from the makeup of ACIP.
Pincus said the organizations would be harmed because federal officials had removed several of them from their longstanding roles as liaison organizations to the committee, limiting their ability to participate in ACIP deliberations.
One judge tested that argument by asking whether the organizations would still be injured if the currently blocked committee met and adopted vaccine recommendations that the plaintiffs themselves supported.
Pincus said they would.
He argued that recommendations produced by a committee lacking the required balance of expertise and viewpoints would lack legitimacy regardless of whether the plaintiffs agreed with the eventual policy result.
The government disputes that reasoning.
It argues that objections to how an advisory committee is constituted do not justify an order preventing presidential administration officials from carrying out appointments before any final agency action has occurred.
The dispute also comes against the backdrop of a recent Supreme Court ruling involving a different federal health advisory body.
In Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, the Supreme Court ruled in June 2025 that members of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force are inferior federal officers who may constitutionally be appointed by the secretary of Health and Human Services.
The administration has cited that ruling in arguing that Kennedy possesses broad authority over appointments to federal health advisory bodies.
The Braidwood decision did not directly decide the separate FACA questions at issue in the ACIP litigation, however.
Murphy’s ruling focused heavily on whether the reconstituted vaccine committee complied with statutory requirements that advisory committees be appropriately balanced and qualified.
His written order said a stay of the appointments was a less drastic remedy than a broader injunction and concluded that the committee’s previous votes should also be suspended because the court had found that ACIP likely violated federal law.
The legal battle grew out of Kennedy’s sweeping restructuring of federal vaccine policy after becoming health secretary.
In June 2025, Kennedy dismissed every member of ACIP, arguing that conflicts of interest had undermined public trust in the panel.
He then installed a new group of advisers, several of whom had previously criticized federal vaccine policies or questioned aspects of vaccine safety and public-health guidance.
The administration described the new membership as bringing greater transparency, independent judgment and a wider range of scientific viewpoints to the committee.
Critics, including major physician organizations, argued that some of the replacements lacked the traditional expertise expected of ACIP members and that the committee had become insufficiently balanced.
The dispute intensified after the reconstituted panel approved changes to federal vaccine recommendations and the administration later announced a significant revision to the childhood immunization schedule.
Murphy temporarily blocked those changes while the lawsuit moves forward.
ACIP plays an influential role in federal health policy because its recommendations affect CDC guidance, insurance coverage requirements and access to vaccines through programs serving children and other patients.
The First Circuit did not immediately rule Tuesday on the government’s request.
Its decision on whether to stay Murphy’s order could determine whether Kennedy is able to restore ACIP and resume meetings while the underlying lawsuit proceeds.
For now, the central appellate question is narrower than the wider political and scientific dispute over vaccine policy: whether the plaintiffs demonstrated enough concrete harm to justify a federal judge stopping the secretary of Health and Human Services from seating his chosen advisers before the legality of those appointments has been finally resolved.

sources.news_title: Appeals Court Questions Judge’s ‘Intrusive’ Order on RFK Jr. Appointments
sources.text:
A federal appeals court on Oct. 6 questioned an order from a U.S. district judge that blocked a panel of vaccine advisers from meeting, as it considers staying the judge’s order.
“What is the harm that needs to be redressed, or that would justify this kind of intrusive relief?” one of the judges on a U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit panel asked during an oral hearing in the case.
Murphy also blocked most of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s appointments to the ACIP committee, determining that many of the members were unqualified and that the committee lacked balance, as required by federal law. Kennedy had removed all ACIP members in 2025, saying they had conflicts of interest, and selected new advisers such as vaccine inventor Dr. Robert Malone and Retsef Levi, a professor of operations management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The committee hasn’t met since.
“We’re asking the court to vacate the order on the appointments so that the secretary can reconstitute the committee and get it back to work,” Matthew Zorn, a government lawyer, told the First Circuit panel on Tuesday.
Zorn said vacating the order would not harm the organizations that sued and would not implicate their interests.
Andrew Pincus, an attorney for the plaintiffs, argued that Murphy entered the “least intrusive relief possible” and that under the order, Kennedy could have re-selected some members and brought some new members on board. “If that constellation of people was lawful, his order would not prohibit that ACIP from going forward,” Pincus said.
Zorn disagreed.
“The practical matter of this case is, the secretary wants to get the ACIP back to work, and we’re being told that if he reconstitutes any committee, it’s going to be right back in court,” he said.
Pincus also argued, in response to a judge wondering what harm the order addressed, that the American Academy of Pediatrics and the other organizations that sued over the schedule changes and appointments would be injured by an unlawfully constituted ACIP meeting because they would not be able to take part since officials removed them as liaison members.
One of the circuit judges on the panel asked whether the plaintiffs would be harmed if ACIP met tomorrow with members whose appointments Murphy stayed and adopted recommendations the plaintiffs want to see.
Yes, Pincus said, because the committee doesn’t have a balance of views to give such a recommendation legitimacy.

sources.news_title: US appeals court weighs block on Kennedy’s vaccine panel appointments
sources.text:
By Nate Raymond
Oct 6 (Reuters) – A lawyer for the Trump administration told a federal appeals court on Tuesday that a judge had improperly hamstrung an influential vaccine advisory panel by blocking Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s handpicked appointees from serving on it.
US Justice Department attorney Matthew Zorn argued at a hearing before the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston that the judge’s ruling was preventing the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices from meeting due to concerns that any new appointments Kennedy made to it could also be blocked.
“We’re asking the court to vacate the order on the appointments so that the secretary can reconstitute the committee and get it back to work,” Zorn said.
Kennedy, an anti-vaccine activist picked by President Donald Trump last year to head the US Department of Health and Human Services, removed and replaced all 17 independent experts who previously served on the panel, which makes recommendations on vaccine policy to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
That action formed the basis of the lawsuit by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical groups, which also sought to block other shifts in vaccine policy under Kennedy.
US District Judge Brian Murphy in a March 16 order concluded that Kennedy, in picking new members, did not comply with the Federal Advisory Committee Act, which requires such advisory panels to be balanced, and instead picked “distinctly unqualified” individuals to serve on the committee that is supposed to be composed of experts on vaccines and immunization.
The Trump administration contends that portion of Murphy’s order has deprived ACIP of a quorum needed to issue recommendations on flu shots and other vaccines because any newly appointed members would likely require court approval.
Some members of the three-judge appeals court panel on Tuesday raised concerns about how Murphy had crafted his order, which blocked 13 appointees from serving. Chief US Circuit Judge David Barron said it lacked any explanation for why blocking Kennedy’s appointees was legally authorized or justified.
“It’s hard to know precisely what harm this relief was designed to address,” he said.
But Andrew Pincus, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, urged the court to leave it in place, saying Murphy’s decision to block 13 of the panel’s members from continuing to serve provided “important protection for America’s public health.”
Murphy in his order also blocked the CDC’s January 5 move to cut the number of routinely recommended childhood vaccinations and set aside votes ACIP had taken under Kennedy’s watch, including to downgrade recommendations for hepatitis B vaccines for newborns and COVID-19 shots broadly.
The Trump administration opted against appealing those portions of that ruling by Murphy, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, and instead focused narrowly on his decision blocking the 13 appointees to the vaccine panel.
Since Murphy ruled, ACIP has not met, canceling two meetings so far. Another, set for October 21-23, would likely also be canceled if the committee is not reconstituted before then.
(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Bill Berkrot)
